name: writing a high-level design
from: A module the architecture names and requirements are allocated to, with nothing between that allocation and code: no unit structure, no interfaces, no data design. Two developers who must meet at a boundary have nowhere to look up what the boundary is.
to: A high-level design: the module decomposed into units, every externally visible interface specified — operations, data, errors — and each unit carrying the requirements allocated to it. A developer can write a unit's low-level design against it without asking the lead what was meant.
cost: The module lead's attention, and the negotiation with neighboring modules that fixing an interface on paper forces — a negotiation that is the work's value and feels like its overhead.
otherwise: Interfaces get decided at the point of first collision, in code, by whichever side got there first — and every later reader takes the accident for a decision.
